8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":3,"verseId":5,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Perception","totalVerses":9,"verseData":{"id":"v3_5","number":5,"title":"Neither Seeing Nor Nonseeing Perceives","sanskrit":{"text":"darśanaṃ tāvad evoktaṃ na paśyaty adarśanaṃ tathā | darśanenaiva cākhyātaḥ draṣṭā samyak prapañcitaḥ ||","transliteration":"darśanaṃ tāvad evoktaṃ na paśyaty adarśanaṃ tathā | darśanenaiva cākhyātaḥ draṣṭā samyak prapañcitaḥ","translation":"Seeing itself does not see. Nonseeing itself does not see. Through seeing itself the clear analysis of the seer is understood."},"philosophy":{"insight":"The abstract concepts \"seeing\" and \"nonseeing\" cannot themselves perceive — neither possesses inherent perceptive power. By analysing seeing itself (showing it can't self-see, has no independent agent), the true nature of the seer is revealed: dependent, empty, and beyond fixed categories.","madhyamaka":"Garfield: this verse draws the conclusion from v.2-4. \"Seeing\" as an abstract act doesn't perceive (it needs conditions). \"Nonseeing\" obviously doesn't perceive. The seer is understood through analysing the process of seeing — and that analysis reveals dependent origination, not inherent existence. Kalupahana: the verse resolves the seer by showing neither extreme (seeing nor nonseeing) captures its nature. Siderits/Katsura note the catuṣkoṭi-like structure: the seer is not defined by seeing, not defined by nonseeing.","quantum":"Wave-Particle Complementarity / Bohr: A quantum entity is neither inherently a wave nor inherently a particle — it manifests as one or the other depending on the experimental context. Neither description alone captures its nature. Understanding comes through analysing the complementary descriptions together, not by fixing one.","bridge":"Both show that fixed categories fail to capture the real nature of their subject. \"Wave\" alone and \"particle\" alone don't describe a quantum entity. \"Seeing\" alone and \"nonseeing\" alone don't describe the seer. In both cases, understanding requires transcending the dichotomy.","accessible":"Is light a wave or a particle? Neither description is complete — it's both depending on context. Similarly, is the seer defined by \"seeing\" or \"nonseeing\"? Neither captures the seer's nature. The seer transcends these fixed categories and exists only as a dependent, relational process.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, we identify seers who see things. Ultimately, the seer cannot be pinned down as either \"seeing\" or \"nonseeing\" — both categories fail to establish its inherent nature.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying the seer is unknowable or mystical. Saying the seer's nature is revealed through analysis as DEPENDENT — not capturable by fixed categories of \"seeing\" or \"nonseeing.\""},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Wave-Particle Complementarity (Bohr)","score":86,"strength":"High","explanation":"Neither \"wave\" nor \"particle\" alone captures quantum nature — both are needed contextually. Parallels the seer transcending \"seeing\"/\"nonseeing\" dichotomy.","caveat":"Structural parallel: both show fixed dichotomies fail. The physics is about measurement contexts; the philosophy is about conceptual categories."},"animation":{"geometry":"Dual-Slit Seer","anchor":"A figure standing before a dual-slit barrier. You need a chef, ingredients, heat, a kitchen. \"Cooking\" as an abstract concept is just a word — it can't make food without the conditions."},{"q":"Why mention \"nonseeing\" at all?","a":"To close the other logical exit.
